newsitem.title: UK: LME copper ends sleepy day touch softer.
newsitem.headline: LME copper ends sleepy day touch softer.

text.p: LME copper was locked in a narrow range on Monday afternoon, taking a rest after attacking the $2,600 per tonne mark last week.
Third Wednesday pricing during the morning rings failed to spark much excitement and three month copper finished the afternoon kerb little changed at $2,588, down $2 from Friday.
In the morning it briefly looked at the downside, hitting a low of $2,565, but spent the afternoon hovering above $2,680.
The market is still overbought and may have trouble rechallenging last week's $2,609 peak in the near-term, analysts said. The 14-day RSI came down only one point on Monday to around 76 percent.
The cash/threes backwardation narrowed to $85/$95 from $95/$100 at the close of business on Friday.
The physical market has been spotty, with some traders reporting buying on the back of a strike at Inco's Sudbury operations, where 4,670 workers walked off the job at midnight on June 2.
Europe is tight with drawdowns from LME warehouses said to be moving to France.
Another physical trader, however, said business has been slow, with consumers wary of buying at high prices ahead of the summer lull.
Traders agreed that demand in Italy was soft and physical premiums had declined about $10 in recent weeks to about $15/$20.
The other metals followed copper's lead, lazily testing the downside.
Nickel chalked up a loss of $90, ending at $7,250, failing to respond to problems at Inco and Norilsk.
The movement has formed a bearish inside day on the charts, indicating further downside pressure.
Some analysts have questioned the strength of demand in the second half, since some stainless mills may need to lower output.
Aluminium was trapped in a tight $8 range between $1,577 and $1,585, ending right in the middle at $1,582, a loss of $4 from Friday's close.
Relentless stock draws have been shrugged off by the market recently, so Monday's erosion of 3,850 tonnes did nothing to encourage prices.
The market is worried that the metal is not going to end-users, but instead to consignment stocks, and also that idled production is being restarted at U.S. plants.
Every recent rally has been capped by producer selling, traders say.
Lead declined by $8 to $621 and may be heading towards its recent $615 lows, traders said.
Tin shed $20 to $5,560 and zinc ended $1 weaker at $1,373.
Alloy finished the kerb $5 easier indicated at $1,475/80.
--Eric Onstad, London Newsroom +44 171 542-8065
